transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. How can I help you today?

Well, thank you. I, um... I drove over from the west side of town this morning, and let me tell you, the construction on Maple Street is just a complete nightmare right now. They've had those orange cones up since October, and nobody seems to be doing any actual work. My neighbor, Susan, she says it's because of a city budget issue, but who knows with the city council these days. 

Anyway, I usually love getting up early. I have these beautiful hydrangeas in the front yard that I've been tending to since I retired, and you have to water them before the sun gets too hot. But lately... well, what actually scared me enough to finally call and ask for help is that I keep having mornings where I just lie in bed and think it might be easier if I just didn't wake up at all. 

I mean, I don't have a plan to hurt myself or anything like that! I wouldn't do that. It's just... the thought is there. And then Susan's dog will start barking next door—he's a terrier mix, very yappy, sweet thing but he just barks at every squirrel—and I just... I don't know, I just wonder why I'm even bothering to get out of bed.
How long have you been feeling this way, with the thoughts about not wanting to wake up and feeling like there's no point?

Well, I suppose it's been about a month now. It started right after my sister died unexpectedly. It was just such a terrible shock to everyone. We had to arrange the funeral so quickly, and let me tell you, dealing with the florist was a whole ordeal in itself. I specifically ordered these beautiful white lilies, because those were her absolute favorite, and they tried to substitute them with carnations! Can you imagine? 

I had to get on the phone with the manager, this very young man who didn't seem to understand why that mattered at all. It really feels like customer service just doesn't exist anymore. Back when I was working—I was an office manager for a logistics company before I retired—if we treated people like that, we'd have been out of business in a week. We always prided ourselves on getting the details right. But... I'm sorry, what was I saying? Oh, right. Yes, it's been about a month since she passed that I've been having those mornings.
Have you noticed that you're not enjoying things as much as you used to, like your hydrangeas or other activities you used to look forward to?

Well, yes, I suppose that's true. I still make myself go to my book club on Tuesdays, and I even went to the community center dance night last week. But... I don't know, lately I just sit there feeling like I'm behind a pane of glass. It's just not the same. 

Actually, at the dance night, they had this new DJ—a young kid, couldn't have been more than twenty—and he kept playing all this electronic noise instead of the classic Motown we usually like. I mean, you can't really do the two-step to whatever that was! Martha, she's the one who usually organizes it, she tried to talk to him, but he just kept fiddling with his laptop. It's like people don't know how to just put on a good record anymore. We used to have such wonderful parties back in the day, real bands with horn sections... 

But anyway, even my garden... I still go out there, but seeing the hydrangeas bloom just doesn't give me that little lift it used to. Same with cooking for the neighbors. I made a casserole for the Smiths next door when their son was visiting, and usually I love doing that, but this time it just felt like... a chore.
Have you been feeling down or depressed most of the day, nearly every day, since your sister passed away?

Well, I suppose I have been feeling rather low most days. It's just this heavy feeling that follows me around. Like when I go to the grocery store... I usually go to the one on 4th Street because they have the best produce section, and I always see Brenda there at the checkout. She's been working there for fifteen years at least, such a lovely woman. Her daughter just graduated from state college, which is wonderful, though I remember when tuition was actually affordable. When I went to get my bachelor's degree, my parents were able to pay for it just from my father's salary at the mill! Now, young people are just drowning in debt before they even start their lives. It's really a shame how things have changed. But yes, to answer your question, I guess I have been feeling down almost every day since she passed.
Have you noticed that you're losing interest in most things you used to enjoy, not just your garden or book club, but other activities too?

Well, I don't really know. I mean, I suppose I haven't been doing much of anything lately. I used to knit quite a bit. I was making this lovely afghan for my niece's new baby—she just had a little boy, Oliver, such a sweet name. Though, honestly, they're raising him with all these screens around. I went over there last month and they had an iPad propped up in front of the high chair! When my sister and I were little, our mother would just give us a wooden spoon and a pot to bang on while she cooked. We turned out just fine. And the toys these days, they're all plastic and need batteries. Whatever happened to good, sturdy wooden blocks? The craftsmanship is just gone. My father used to carve the most beautiful little animals for us out of pine... 

But, oh, I'm sorry. What were you asking me about? My activities? I guess I just haven't really noticed if I'm losing interest in other things. I just haven't felt like doing much of anything.
Have you noticed that you feel more tired or have less energy than usual, nearly every day, since your sister passed away?

Well, yes, I have been. Every day it just feels like... well, even doing simple errands or trying to get my papers together for the Cultural Center, it leaves me feeling completely worn out. It's honestly like my body is moving through thick mud. 

And I really need to get those papers sorted because the Center is planning the spring gala, and I've kept all the old programs and committee notes from the past decade. You know, back in 2015, we managed to book this absolutely wonderful string quartet from the city. They played Vivaldi, and let me tell you, the acoustics in that old heritage hall are just magnificent. They really don't construct buildings like that anymore, with real lath and plaster and solid oak floors. Nowadays everything is just drywall and that cheap grey laminate flooring. My neighbor, Mr. Henderson, he just redid his entire kitchen in that grey laminate, and it already looks so terribly drab. I told him he should have gone with a warm, natural wood, but people just buy whatever is trendy on those home renovation television shows. It's a shame, really, how everything is so disposable now. There's no sense of permanence. 

But, oh, I'm rambling again. My energy, you said? Yes, I just feel very tired all the time.
Have you noticed that your movements or speech have been slower or more restless than usual lately?

Well, I haven't really noticed anything like that. My speech seems fine to me, I think. Though, speaking of talking, I was on the phone with my cousin Martha yesterday. She lives down in Florida now, moved there about five years ago to get away from the winters up here. I don't blame her, really, the snow shoveling gets to be too much at our age. But she was telling me about her new neighbor who just moved in from New York, and apparently, the woman talks a mile a minute! Martha says she can barely get a word in edgewise when they run into each other at the mailbox. I always thought that was just a stereotype about New Yorkers, you know, being in such a rush all the time. But I suppose there's some truth to it. 

When my late husband and I visited the city back in the eighties, we couldn't believe how fast everyone walked. We were just trying to admire the architecture—those beautiful old brownstones—and people were practically shoving us out of the way on the sidewalk. It's just a different pace of life, I suppose. Not like here, where people actually take the time to say hello and ask about your day. I much prefer our quiet little town, even if the winters are harsh. 

Anyway, what was it you asked? Slower movements? I don't think so, no. I just haven't noticed anything like that.
Have you been feeling like you’re not worth much or that you’ve been blaming yourself for things more than usual?

Well, yes, I suppose I have been. I just keep going over and over those last few weeks with my sister in my head. I keep telling myself I should have called her more, that I should have listened better, or just done something more useful for her. Even when part of me knows I couldn't have changed what happened, I just feel so terribly guilty about the phone calls. 

Though, speaking of calling, it really is so easy to stay in touch now with these smart phones, isn't it? When my sister and I were girls, we shared this heavy, avocado-green rotary phone that sat out in the main hallway. It was on one of those little telephone tables with a built-in seat—you really never see those anymore. My mother kept a beautiful lace doily under the phone that she crocheted herself. Everyone had doilies back then to protect the wood from getting scratched. Now people just buy that cheap flat-pack furniture from that Swedish store and they don't even care if it gets ruined because they'll just throw it out in a year anyway. It's so terrible for the landfills, all that particle board and glue just sitting there. When my late husband and I got married, we saved up for a solid cherry dining set, and it still looks completely brand new, even after all the Thanksgiving dinners we hosted over the years. You just had to polish it twice a year with a good beeswax...

Oh, I'm so sorry. I completely lost my train of thought again. You were asking if I was blaming myself for things? Yes, I just feel awful about those last few weeks with her.
Have your symptoms been present for most of the day, nearly every day, since your sister passed away?

Well, yes, I suppose it has. It's been about a month now, ever since she passed away so unexpectedly. It just feels like every day is the same since then. 

Though, you know, a month doesn't sound like a long time, but it really can feel like an eternity when you're just sitting in the house. I was looking at the calendar in my kitchen yesterday—it's one of those beautiful Thomas Kinkade calendars with the little cottages and the glowing windows. My sister always used to buy me one for Christmas every year. She loved his paintings. Some people say they're a bit too sentimental, but I think they're just lovely. They remind me of the little cottage we used to rent on the lake when we were children. We would spend the whole month of July up there, and my father would take us out in this old aluminum rowboat to fish for sunnies. You don't see those old aluminum boats much anymore, either. Now everyone has those fiberglass speedboats with the massive engines that make so much noise you can barely hear yourself think, let alone enjoy the peace and quiet of the water. It really ruins the atmosphere for everyone else on the lake, just zooming back and forth and kicking up such a wake that it erodes the shoreline. The loons don't even nest in the same spots they used to because of all the commotion. 

But... oh dear, I've wandered off again, haven't I? I'm sorry. You were asking if it's been every day? Yes, for about a month now, since she died. Every single day.
Have you noticed any changes in your appetite or weight recently, such as eating much less or more than usual, or losing or gaining weight without trying?

Well, you know, food just doesn't call to me much anymore. I'll fix a little toast or maybe heat up some soup, and then I'll realize by evening that I've barely eaten anything all day. And I'm certainly not trying to lose weight, it's just... I don't know, the desire just isn't there. 

Speaking of soup, though, I used to make the most wonderful chicken noodle soup from scratch. My mother taught me how to make the broth by simmering the bones for hours with celery and carrots. You really can't get that kind of flavor from a can, no matter what those commercials say. Have you seen the price of groceries lately, by the way? I was at the market on Tuesday to pick up some tea, and the cost of a simple loaf of bread is just outrageous. It's no wonder people don't bake anymore. When I was young, the smell of fresh bread baking was just a normal part of the week. My grandmother had this beautiful old cast-iron Dutch oven she used for her sourdough. It weighed an absolute ton, but it baked the most perfect, crusty loaves. People today use those fancy electric bread machines, but I always thought they took the soul right out of baking. There's something about kneading the dough by hand, feeling it change texture... 

Oh, my goodness, I'm doing it again, aren't I? I'm so sorry, doctor. You asked about my appetite? Yes, I've just been having a little toast or soup, really. I just haven't been eating much at all.

Oh, my goodness, I'm doing it again, aren't I? I'm so sorry, doctor. You asked about my appetite? Yes, I've just been having a little toast or soup, really. I just haven't been eating much at all.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with a first-episode, severe major depressive episode following the death of her sister. While the symptoms are temporally related to a bereavement, the presence of persistent depressed mood, anhedonia, fatigue, feelings of worthlessness/guilt, and reduced appetite, occurring nearly every day for approximately one month, meets criteria for a major depressive episode. The severity is classified as severe due to the presence of suicidal ideation (though without intent or plan), significant functional impairment, and marked anhedonia.
